clinicalPearls: Causes brief paroxysms of severe pain felt deep in the ear canal, sometimes radiating to the auricle, soft palate, or over the face
A trigger zone in the posterior wall of the external auditory canal is characteristic, with attacks provoked by touching the canal or by swallowing
Because the nervus intermedius carries taste, lacrimal, and salivary fibres, attacks may be associated with altered taste, lacrimation, or salivation
It is closely related to, and often used synonymously with, geniculate neuralgia, both reflecting neuralgia of the sensory division of the facial nerve
A varicella-zoster (herpetic) origin is recognised and it may follow Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Diagnosis requires exclusion of primary ear disease, glossopharyngeal and trigeminal neuralgia, and structural posterior fossa lesions
First-line treatment is anticonvulsant medication such as carbamazepine; microvascular decompression or nervus intermedius section is reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Nervus intermedius neuralgia is a paroxysmal pain disorder of the nervus intermedius, the sensory and parasympathetic branch of the facial nerve. Its sensory fibres, relaying via the geniculate ganglion, supply a small area of the external auditory canal and auricle, which explains the deep-ear pain. Ectopic, hyperexcitable neural activity, attributed to vascular compression at the root entry zone or to prior herpetic inflammation of the ganglion, generates the lancinating paroxysms. The nerve's parasympathetic and taste functions account for accompanying lacrimation, salivation, and gustatory disturbance during attacks, and its anatomical intimacy with the facial, glossopharyngeal, and trigeminal nerves produces overlapping presentations.
additionalDifferentials: Primary otological disease (otitis externa or media)
Referred otalgia from a head and neck malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and microscopy to exclude external and middle ear disease
MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle focused on the facial nerve
MR angiography to detect a compressive vascular loop
Testing of the external auditory canal for a triggerable zone
Examination of the pharynx and larynx to exclude referred otalgia from malignancy
Audiometry if hearing symptoms accompany the pain
redFlags: Auricular vesicles with facial weakness suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Persistent unilateral otalgia with a normal ear prompting a search for a head and neck primary
A cerebellopontine angle mass on imaging
Progressive facial nerve weakness or additional cranial neuropathies
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but distressing; many patients respond to anticonvulsant therapy, and surgical decompression or sectioning of the nervus intermedius provides relief in selected refractory cases.
pitfalls: Attributing deep-ear pain to primary ear disease when the ear is normal
Not distinguishing it from, or conflating it with, glossopharyngeal neuralgia
Failing to exclude referred otalgia from an occult malignancy
Missing a treatable vascular loop or posterior fossa lesion on imaging
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line medical therapy is with an anticonvulsant such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine to suppress the neuralgic paroxysms
Add or substitute other neuropathic agents such as gabapentin, pregabalin or baclofen if response is inadequate or the first agent is not tolerated
Where a herpetic (varicella-zoster) origin or preceding Ramsay Hunt syndrome is identified, treat with antiviral therapy
Consider microvascular decompression of the nervus intermedius where a compressive vascular loop is demonstrated in drug-refractory cases
Offer sectioning of the nervus intermedius, with the geniculate ganglion, as a surgical option for disabling, treatment-resistant pain
Confirm the diagnosis by excluding primary ear disease, glossopharyngeal and trigeminal neuralgia and structural posterior fossa lesions, with neurology and otolaryngology referral
